item.title: Relic and Gumi: Governing Memory, Safety, and Continuity in Diegetic Relational Agents
item.description: arXiv:2611.08504v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Longitudinal relational agents rely on memory for continuity, but remembering can lead to intrusion, clinical overconfidence, emotional manipulation, and opacity. We present Relic, a governance architecture for diegetic relational agents, and Gumi, a subject-specific companion agent initialized and governed through Relic. The architecture separates what the system can observe, what researchers can review, what Gumi can remember, and what Gumi can say. We describe three mechanisms. Relic represents sensitive safety signals as researcher-facing governance objects rather than user-facing explanations or agent memories. Shared Continuity Memory organizes relational markers around subject-confirmed wording, corrections, explicit follow-up permissions, and recall limits. We specify a runtime mediation layer for delivery, proactivity, session identity, output transformation, and platform allowlists; adoption across live paths remains partial. These mechanisms aim to preserve relational continuity without turning Gumi into a clinical assistant, mood tracker, general-purpose assistant, or opaque profiling system. We contribute the architecture, object model, researcher workbench design, and a proposed evaluation framework for governed relational memory. An exploratory pilot involved the author as P1 and one external participant as P2. Weekly self-reports from P1 and researcher-led interviews with P2 provide descriptive observations of early use and perceived naturalness. The pilot does not support claims about clinical efficacy, diagnosis, therapeutic outcomes, general usability, or deployment safety. Relic provides research infrastructure intended to make relational memory, safety constraints, and agent behavior inspectable and testable.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Veri'

item.title: Seeing Is Not Knowing: The Epistemic Limits of LLM-Based Mental Health Inference from Youth Social Media Conversations
item.description: arXiv:2611.08565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adolescents increasingly use social media for private conversations, sharing experiences and seeking support. These interactions generate digital traces, prompting efforts to infer mental health and psychosocial states. As large language models become more capable of reasoning about conversations and interpersonal dynamics, a fundamental question remains nonetheless: what can models actually "know" about an individual's psychological experience from what they are able to "see"? We evaluated ten reasoning LLMs using donated Instagram Direct Messages from 80 adolescents with a history of depression or suicidal thoughts and behaviors, comparing predictions with self-reports and analyzing 204 reasoning traces. Models performed better when inferring more observable states than participants' subjective appraisals of social experience, such as perceived social support. Beyond prediction accuracy, our findings highlight the epistemic limits of digital traces for AI design and evaluation: what can be observed, what can reasonably be inferred, and what requires people's own accounts.
item.dc:creator: Xiaohan Ding, Mengting Tu, Andrew H. Zhao, Jamie Zelazny, Candice L. Biernesser, Munmun De Choudhury

item.title: Goals as a Representational Layer for Human-AI Collaboration
item.description: arXiv:2611.08757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Goals are central to how people, teams, and organizations structure their work. Yet, while generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly operate across a worker's context, information about why a person is pursuing a task, beyond local prompts and interactions, is typically missing. We argue that goals should become an explicit representational layer mediating interactions among people, AI systems, and organizations. Because human goals are hierarchical, partially latent, and dynamically evolving, such a layer must be multidimensional, both grounded in human articulation and inferred from available evidence, and continuously updated. A goal layer could connect immediate requests to broader outcomes, improve the organization and retrieval of relevant context, support reflection and coordination, and provide a foundation for training, aligning, and evaluating AI systems in terms of human-centered outcomes. We highlight these opportunities while identifying open challenges involving goal inference, socio-cognitive frictions, alignment, privacy, and governance.
item.dc:creator: Gaia Molinaro, Lev Tankelevitch, Sean Rintel, Scott Counts

item.title: Learning from How Users Interpret: Personalizing Recommendation Explanation Order
item.description: arXiv:2611.08785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personalized explanations typically adapt their content or presentation based on preferences, interaction histories, or other user characteristics. We examine whether regularities inferred from prior textual interpretations can support personalization of explanation organization. In a controlled within participant study with 122 participants, prior interpretations were represented along three dimensions: information selection, relative salience, and relational organization. The relational dimension was partially operationalized through co mobilization. These representations were aggregated into fixed historical profiles and used to organize otherwise identical explanation sentences. Participants encountered four organization procedures: the OWN historical profile, the DONOR historical profile, a population profile called POP, and a language model procedure using the historical profile called PROFILE LLM. Post exposure objective comprehension was the primary outcome. OWN achieved 86.5 percent correct responses, compared with 66.0 percent for DONOR, 63.9 percent for POP, and 73.0 percent for PROFILE LLM. Mixed effects analyses showed higher comprehension with OWN than with each alternative procedure. No reliable overall condition effect was detected for recommendation acceptance. These findings indicate that historical profiles derived from prior interpretations can provide an actionable signal for personalizing explanation order while keeping explanatory content and wording fixed.
item.dc:creator: Deo Munduku, Elsa Negre

item.title: MotionDecipher: LLM-Assisted Clinical Interpretation of Human Motion Signals for Efficient Gait Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.08795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical gait and motion analysis is widely used to guide targeted interventions for patients with neurological disorders, the outcome of which is typically a report with descriptions of joint movements and forces. Current practices rely on experts' manual effort, which is labor-intensive and time-consuming. Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) provide opportunities to address this problem, but translating human motion into clinical gait descriptions remains challenging because the quality of the context directly affects LLMs' reasoning capability over continuous motion signals. To tackle this, we introduce MotionDecipher, a novel framework bridging the semantic gap between motion data and clinical interpretations. Specifically, we made 3 key advancements: 1) a Human Motion Tokenizer that converts motion signals into domain-specific tokens for time- and frequency-informed gait interpretation; 2) a Meta Feature Selector that transforms tokens into Structured Representations; and 3) a Hybrid Context Constructor to determine the optimal demonstration-based prompt for In-Context Learning. We evaluated MotionDecipher on data collected at an accredited gait lab from 122 patients and 46 controls. Results show that MotionDecipher achieves 0.91 BERTScore (13% over GPT-5), while expert evaluation ranks MotionDecipher highest in Correctness, Completeness, and Conciseness compared to baselines, highlighting its promise for efficient gait analysis.
item.dc:creator: Mingrui Ma, Tian Tan, Jinsi Guo, Jessica Rose, Yiwen Dong

item.title: Driver Takeovers and Longitudinal Responses Analysis from Naturalistic Driving
item.description: arXiv:2611.08798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As Level 2 advanced driver-assistance systems (ADAS) become more widely used, understanding driver-system interaction is increasingly important for traffic safety. However, limited real-world data make these interactions difficult to study. We present ADAS-TO, a naturalistic dataset of 16,446 takeover clips from 364 drivers across 2,585 different drives. It combines road video, vehicle kinematics, driver inputs, and ADAS status. To analyze takeover behavior, we retained 6,206 manually reviewed takeover events during continued lane keeping or car following. We excluded events in which the driver intentionally changed lanes, turned, or made a stop beyond the ADAS's capabilities (e.g., at a red light or stop sign) shortly after takeover. Drivers began intervening before ADAS disengaged in 65.6% of takeovers involving braking or steering. When the ego vehicle was still closing on a lead vehicle at disengagement, longitudinal safety margins often narrowed further after the transfer to manual control. Among 2,031 such events, 78.5% had a lower minimum time-to-collision (TTC) in the five seconds after disengagement than in the five seconds before it. For events involving braking, the mean TTC trajectory reached its minimum about 1.2 s after disengagement. We model the subsequent braking response using a Gazis-Herman-Rothery (GHR) car-following law. Its median five-second spacing root-mean-square error is 1.34 m with observed lead motion and 1.84 m with predicted lead motion. The fitted model expresses braking as a response to looming, with stronger responses at higher speeds and shorter gaps. Applied before takeover, it shows that greater looming than predicted by the human-response reference is associated with disengagement. These findings support continued assessment of longitudinal safety after ADAS disengagement, while the driver's braking response develops.
item.dc:creator: Yuhang Wang, Hao Zhou

item.title: Lea: An Agent Backbone for Mathematician-Controlled Formalization in Lean
item.description: arXiv:2611.08849v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic systems now formalize research-level mathematics in Lean, but they are built for autonomy: the mathematician states a target and inspects a result. The alternative, a general-purpose coding harness, is domain-neutral and must be assembled into a formalization workspace before any mathematics begins. Mathematicians, however, report wanting to keep high-level control over how an argument is decomposed and established. We present $\textbf{Lea}$, a Lean-specific agent backbone for mathematician-facing software rather than a single interface. Lea exposes runs, sessions, and typed events through one application-neutral API, and ships with Lean tooling (blueprints, LSP, Loogle, SafeVerify) already wired. We report two applications built on it: $\textbf{LeaChat}$, a web client for interactive proof authoring, and $\textbf{LeaOverleaf}$, which formalizes theorems annotated directly in an Overleaf document; a session begun in either continues in the other. In a case study, a mathematician outlined a proof of the Durfee square generating function in a few natural-language messages, and Lea produced a complete Lean development from Mathlib alone, following the intended decomposition closely and requiring substantive correction at a single point. Lea and both applications are released as open source so that further mathematician-facing tools can be built on the same backbone.
item.dc:creator: Shaswat Patel, Daniel Aarao Reis Arturi, Kevin Gomez, Jaume de Dios Pont, Jorge Poco, Eduardo V. Teixeira, Sam Westrick, Claudio Silva, Chinmay Hegde

item.title: "I had nobody to turn to": Why LGBTQ+ People Choose (Not) to Use AI Chatbots for Personal Health and Relationship Advice
item.description: arXiv:2611.08854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While there is an abundance of research into large language model (LLM) biases against LGBTQ+ communities, far less research has examined how and why LGBTQ+ people choose to make use of AI chatbots. In this work, we examine how LGBTQ+ people choose (not) to use AI chatbots across three domains in which LGBTQ+ users have unique needs: relationship support, mental health support, and gender or sexual health support. We surveyed 73 people (60 LGBTQ+; 13 non-LGBTQ+) on how they interact with AI chatbots and find that participants' access to external resources, privacy concerns, and perceptions of chatbot capabilities shape whether and how they choose to make use of AI chatbots. For instance, some LGBTQ+ participants felt that chatbots might actually be less biased against LGBTQ+ people than the people they know offline. We also find that LGBTQ+ participants report using AI chatbots less frequently than non-LGBTQ+ participants across 15 specific personal health and relationship advice scenarios, citing concerns about AI sycophancy and adverse cognitive side-effects. Recognizing AI chatbots as vital (albeit imperfect) resources for LGBTQ+ people, we recommend researchers consider systemic issues that drive users to AI chatbots and design technologies (AI or otherwise) that prioritize privacy, anonymity, and real human connection.
item.dc:creator: Jacob Hobbs, Ashray Gupta, Dennis Ulmer, Geetanjali Aich, Nolan Golden, Yanan Long, Ian Rios-Sialer, Jennifer Mickel, Morgan Klaus Scheuerman, Rohit Avinash Mujumdar, Virginia K. Felkner, Jordan Taylor, William Agnew

item.title: Bidirectional Modeling of mmWave Human Signals for Enhancement & Synthesis
item.description: arXiv:2611.08870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Millimeter-wave (mmWave) is attractive for human-centered robotics in smoke, darkness, and privacy-sensitive indoor spaces: it measures reflections rather than visually identifiable imagery and remains usable without light. Deployed systems, however, face two complementary needs that run in opposite directions. Enhancement starts from a raw range-angle-Doppler (RAD) heatmap, where human returns coexist with nonhuman structure, and aims to isolate the human signal by removing nonhuman returns, yielding a clean RAD input for downstream perception. Synthesis starts from denser human geometry and aims to synthesize natural RAD observations, including environmental and hardware features, thereby expanding scarce supervision data. Although the two tasks reverse direction, both require modeling how human and nonhuman reflections coexist in the same measurement. Among RAD axes, Doppler provides motion information native to the modality, with the potential to support this modeling. We therefore cast both tasks on the dual-domain RAD heatmap and propose HeatWave, which injects Doppler when it is locally reliable, and routes Doppler asymmetrically for enhancement and synthesis within one shared backbone. This design improves both tasks: enhanced observations reduce mean per-joint position error by 11.4% relative to the raw recording, and synthesized samples that replace half of the real radar labels recover most of the activity accuracy lost to the reduced budget. Relative to an unspecialized dual-task heatmap baseline, the enhancement improves motion-critical samples under metallic clutter by 2.3times more than when geometry already suffices, and synthesis follows the same ordering with a narrower spread, providing the community with a research direction more closely aligned with the signal's characteristics.
item.dc:creator: Shuntian Zheng, Hoang Hai Pham, Jiaqi Li, Xiaoman Lu, Shuai He, Yu Guan

item.title: The Relational Capacity Framework: A Lens for AI-Mediated Relationality
item.description: arXiv:2611.08877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A growing literature examines the impact of engaging with AI chatbots on our relationality: our ability to form relationships with others, maintain them through life's changes, and exit when needed. Currently, substantial work focuses on purpose-built AI companions (e.g. Replika, Character.AI), with less work investigating socioemotional uses of the more widely-used general-purpose chatbots. In this paper, we present a 100-person investigation into how people engage general-purpose AI for socioemotional needs. Participants' AI uses varied, from practicing specific social skills to seeking additional bandwidth and information as they navigated their social contexts. To explain this heterogeneity, we provide 8 states that describe how AI expands or contracts relationality for people with different levels of skills, bandwidth, and information. We then present a unified conceptual model for the role of technology in mediating human relationality, the Relational Capacity Framework, and outline future research designing appropriate roles for AI in human connection.
item.dc:creator: Emily Tseng, Patrick Gage Kelley, Renee Shelby, Ashley M. Walker

item.title: The Drawing You Watch Is the Portrait You Keep: A Replayable Machine Portrait Studio
item.description: arXiv:2611.08994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ask an image model for your portrait and a finished picture arrives: no first line, no second thoughts, no record of how it got there, and a different picture if you ask again. I built a portrait studio that works the other way. A sitter chooses one of eight fictional artists, each written with a city, a medium and a tempo of its own, holds still for 8 to 12 seconds, and watches a drawing of themselves appear over 44 seconds. One still is sent after consent, a hosted image model returns a private study the sitter never sees, and a compiler turns that study into one drawing document. The live drawing, the saved sheet, the vector export and the film all read that document, and a replay makes no model call, so the drawing you watch is the portrait you keep. I describe the compiler in enough detail to rebuild it and say plainly what it is: an authored reconstruction at a compressed speed, not a recorded hand. On 16 generated test studies a sheet holds 8,784 to 16,378 timed contacts, about three quarters of them fixed-grid fills and nearly all shorter than one video frame, and recompiling one study gave byte-identical output four times on one machine. The paper also traces a bug that matters more than any of that. The earlier compiler estimated the paper colour tile by tile, read dark skin as paper, and in all eight hands kept less of a deep-complexioned face than a fair one (13 to 48 percent against 41 to 56). On 80 generated studies the rebuilt engine keeps the complexion difference the study already has (raw retention 89 to 120 percent), so the fairness question has moved upstream, to the study and the hosted model. The two test sitters are generated and differ in more than complexion, and no real-face or perceptual study exists yet. The studio is live at https://everyfaceproject.com.
item.dc:creator: Vinod Rajpurohit

item.title: "Despite her age, Margaret was eager to make a change": Unpacking Aging Representations and Stereotypes in LLM-generated Stories
item.description: arXiv:2611.09043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly generate everyday stories, their portrayals can shape expectations about aging. Prior work has largely examined age stereotypes in short responses, leaving unanswered whose lives models default to imagining and how age shapes characters' roles in complete narratives. We analyze 594 stories generated by Gemini, GPT, and Llama using text embeddings, LLM-assisted coding, and qualitative analysis. When age was unspecified, stories typically featured younger adults, with middle-aged protagonists largely absent. Older adults were often portrayed through loss, familiar routines, and help from younger characters. Even positive stories sometimes treated older adults' achievements as surprising or portrayed others making decisions on their behalf. We suggest evaluating not only the tone of generated stories, but also who appears, what opportunities they receive, and who makes decisions. Involving older adults in these evaluations can guide writing tools toward more varied, less stereotyped portrayals of later life.
item.dc:creator: MD. Roqunuzzaman Sojib, Mohammad Sadat Hossain, Nafis Tahmid, Shattik Islam Rhythm, Novia Nurain

item.title: Rhythmic Fitness Beat 'Em All using Real-Time Monocular Human Pose Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2611.09228v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Short and frequent physical activity exercices mitigate the health risks of sedentary behavior. Yet, the lack of motivation remains a critical barrier to adoption. Exergames gamify physical activity, but most rely on dedicated hardware, and outside dance and rhythm games they rarely use the musical beat. We present a work-in-progress beat 'em up exergame played with the whole body in front of a single smartphone, which runs the entire pipeline: an off-the-shelf real-time 3D human mesh recovery model on the phone's neural processing unit, gesture recognition, and the game, shown on any TV through a USB-C to HDMI cable. Our contributions are (1) a 3D recognition of five shadow-boxing moves (guard, punch, slip, squat, jump), each defined by one metric measure in a body frame aligned with gravity and one threshold with hysteresis, personalised during a tutorial; (2) a rhythm stage whose discrete cues are placed on the song's kick drum and judged on the movement's capture time, with a delay learned for each player; and (3) a phone-only architecture, running at 30 frames per second, that turns a phone and an HDMI cable into an exergame console.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: International Conference on Entertainment Computing 2026, Oct 2026, Paris CNAM, France
item.dc:creator: Yanis Zaoui (I3SP - URP3625), Valentin B\'egel (I3SP - URP3625), Mohamed Adjel

item.title: Thinking Twice: A Sequential Approach to Nudge Towards Reflective Judgment in GenAI-Assisted Decision Making
item.description: arXiv:2611.09269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humans increasingly use generative AI (GenAI) for decision-making assistance, yet tend to engage in such situations using quick, intuitive (System 1) rather than deliberate, analytical assessment (System 2) as reflected in Dual Process Theory. Such engagement reduces the effectiveness of human-GenAI interactions and increases associated risks. Our research investigates how to design human-GenAI interactions that promote the transition from System 1 to System 2 thinking in decision-making. Based on the Three-Stage-Model, which suggests humans switch to System 2 when conflicts are detected, we conducted an experiment (n=130) testing sequential human-GenAI interaction as a cognitive forcing nudge during problem-solving tasks. This approach, where humans decide first before receiving AI assistance, enables detection of conflicting decisions. Compared to non-sequential settings (concurrent or no AI assistance), results show the sequential condition significantly enhanced both decision performance and GenAI prompt utilization, providing valuable insights for designing more reflective and thus effective human-GenAI interactions.
item.dc:creator: H\"useyin Hussein Keke, Daniel Eisenhardt, Christian Meske

item.title: Sensed but Not Told: Hidden Physiological Adaptation Shapes LLM Persuasion
item.description: arXiv:2611.09394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Wearable sensors, including those embedded in VR headsets, can provide LLM-based chatbots with physiological signals that users do not explicitly communicate. We tested whether such hidden input changes persuasion. In a $2\times2$ within-subjects study ($N=24$), a chatbot argued against participants' self-selected opinions with or without turn-level heart-rate and pupil-diameter features; sensing was disclosed halfway through the study. Before disclosure, sensing increased perceived persuasiveness by 1.42 points. Across the study, sensing was associated with a 0.57-point greater shift toward the chatbot's position and 3.20 times the odds of any movement toward it. Persuasiveness ratings were lower after disclosure, although disclosure was confounded with session order. Dialogue logs suggested a more declarative interaction style when sensing was on: chatbot replies contained question marks less often, and conversations contained fewer turns. These findings motivate making biosignal-driven adaptation inspectable and providing a genuinely non-sensed mode.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyan Wei, Yutong Qu, Yutong Li, Haiyi Li, Wei Emma Zhang, Hsiang-Ting Chen

item.title: DeepRadio: A Human-Agent Workspace for Physical Radio Development
item.description: arXiv:2611.09418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic programming can automate software-defined radio (SDR) development, but decisions can propagate from software to hardware without sufficient user visibility or control. We present DeepRadio, a human-agent workspace embedded in GNU Radio Companion (GRC) for jointly constructing, verifying, and operating physical radio systems. DeepRadio uses a dynamic and state-driven workflow to coordinate a traceable radio specification, claim-oriented cross-layer verification, and mixed-initiative control. These mechanisms expose decisions, tie conclusions to available evidence, and return control to users before consequential hardware actions. Across seven atomic SDR tasks, DeepRadio completed nearly all runs while satisfying all prescribed software and radio-frequency constraints. In a 20-participant study, more participants achieved a verified physical deployment with DeepRadio than with Codex-assisted GRC. Participants reported stronger support for shared intent and understanding while retaining initiative and control. These results suggest that DeepRadio can make agent-assisted physical radio development more reliable, understandable, and controllable.
item.dc:creator: Jiazhen Lei, Yuxin Sha, Sihan Wang, Wenhui Li, Jinyang Sun, Chengyu Lu, Xiaohua Tian

item.title: Entering a New Domain in the Era of Generative AI: An Autoethnography of Solo Game Development as a Bioinformatics Educator
item.description: arXiv:2611.09623v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid improvement of generative AI (GenAI) not only increased the efficiency of practice but also empowered individuals with capabilities to explore new domains. However, identity formation in the wake of such empowerment remains understudied. We use an autoethnography to understand identity formation in the context of solo game development as a bioinformatics educator. With the goal of developing a create-your-own-adventure (CYOA) game, we collected data for 73 days through journal entries, interacting with communities of practices. The autoethnographer had continuously reassessed the situation, and closely interacted with communities of practice. Their prior knowledge was used to provide in-game context and to uniquely interpret game development processes. These findings suggest that the autoethnographer made efforts to belong to communities of practice and engaged extensively in sensemaking through the lens of a bioinformatics educator. Although GenAI puts power at hand, attaining a new identity took place at a human pace.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Kim

item.title: GroundWork: Bridging Human and LLM Reasoning Through a Structured Argumentation Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.09840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into workflows that require reasoning over text documents, yet interaction remains largely conversational. This leaves argumentative structure implicit or embedded in text, making it difficult to maintain, compare, and revise arguments as analyses evolve. We present GroundWork, a mixed-initiative system that makes argument structure a shared, editable state for humans and LLMs. GroundWork operationalizes the Toulmin model of argumentation as a typed graph with explicit operations for human and LLM edits. It exposes this structure through coordinated corpus views and an editable workbench for constructing, comparing, testing, and tracing source-grounded arguments. We evaluate GroundWork through an expert study with four participants spanning consulting, product development, law, and immunology, and three use-case scenarios in intelligence, law, and medicine. Our findings show that GroundWork makes source-grounded arguments inspectable, comparable, and revisable as shared human-LLM state.
item.dc:creator: Sjoerd Vink, Byungmoo Kim, Michael Behrisch, Adam Coscia, Remco Chang

item.title: Investigating Anthropometric Fidelity in SAM 3D Body
item.description: arXiv:2601.06035v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The release of SAM 3D Body is a recent development in human mesh recovery, demonstrating improved performance in producing clean, topologically coherent meshes from single images. By leveraging the Momentum Human Rig (MHR), it achieves robustness to occlusion and diverse poses. However, our evaluation reveals a specific and consistent limitation: the model struggles to reconstruct detailed anthropometric deviations, particularly in populations exhibiting distinctive morphological alterations such as geriatric muscle atrophy, scoliosis, or pregnancy, even when these features are prominent in the input image. In this paper, we investigate this phenomenon not as a failure of the model's capacity, but as a byproduct of the "perception-distortion trade-off". We posit that the architectural reliance on the low-dimensional parametric MHR representation, combined with semantic-invariant conditioning (DINOv3) and annotation-based alignment, creates a pervasive "regression to the mean" effect. We analyze these mechanisms to understand why individual biological details are smoothed out. Furthermore, we state our contributions by proposing specific, constructive pathways for future work, such as implicit-explicit hybrid representations and Medical-in-the-Loop alignment, to extend the baseline performance of SAM 3D Body into the high-precision medical domain.
item.dc:creator: Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Ruting Cheng, James Hahn

item.title: "A Space Where I Can Be Myself": Exploring Safe Visibility for Graduate Student Mothers in Mom Cafes
item.description: arXiv:2611.08710v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Graduate student mothers navigate intertwined demands of graduate study and caregiving, yet little is known about how they seek support through online communities. We examine this through Mom Cafes, locally based online parenting communities in South Korea. Drawing on focus group interviews and design workshops with 22 graduate student mothers, we identify a pattern of dual invisibility: caregiving circumstances were difficult to make legible in academic contexts, while academic circumstances were difficult to make legible in parenting contexts. Although Mom Cafes offered useful local information and emotional reassurance, concerns specific to graduate student motherhood were harder to articulate or safely disclose. Participants sought ways to make graduate student motherhood recognizable when relevant, but their designs highlighted tensions around identifiability, judgment, relational burden and accountability. We conceptualize these tensions as safe visibility and discuss infrastructures for selective recognition, low-obligation connection, and accountable pathways to practical care.
item.dc:creator: Jeanne Choi, Joohee Choi, Jeong-woo Jang

item.title: What Limits mmWave Human-State Sensing for Robot Perception?
item.description: arXiv:2611.08863v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Assistive robots and search-and-rescue platforms require reliable human state sensing in smoke, darkness, and privacy-sensitive environments, where cameras and LiDAR may be unreliable Millimeter-wave radar offers an alternative that works without ambient light, penetrates smoke, and does not capture visual appearance. However, the compact arrays that fit robot size, power, and cost budgets have limited apertures, producing joint-localization errors on the order of decimeters at a few meters, large enough to compromise the safety margins and tracking accuracy a robot depends on. Existing pipelines reduce pose error through frame fusion, multiple viewpoints, return selection, or stronger estimators, but examine one technique at a time, without relating its effect to a shared measurement limit or separating gains from added information from gains from estimator completion. We address this gap with a framework that models the human and environment as one time-varying scattering field and states a Cramer-Rao type error floor for joint localization as a function of bandwidth, aperture, signal-to-noise ratio, fused frame count, phase coherence, and visibility of retained returns. We then use existing frame fusion, multi viewpoint, return selection, and pose estimation methods as matched probes of this floor rather than as competing pipelines. Under the evaluated conditions, experiments on three datasets and a live deployment show these strategies move joint localization error in the predicted directions, for example lowering mean per-joint position error from about 97 to 65 mm with a second viewpoint, while a stronger estimator mainly lowers overall error by completing joints the measurement cannot resolve. These results give the robotics community a principled basis for deciding whether to prioritize observation design or estimator capacity when deploying reliable mmWave human sensing.
item.dc:creator: Shuntian Zheng, Guangming Wang, Hongyang He, Shuai He, Yu Guan

item.title: EventHOI: Event-Driven Resource-Efficient Hand-Object Interaction Logging on Smartglasses
item.description: arXiv:2611.09089v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hand-object interactions (HOIs) can be captured by smartglasses to learn how people manipulate objects in daily life. Automatic logging of these interactions from an egocentric perspective provides time-stamped evidence of daily actions for applications like memory assistance. However, continuous RGB capture and wireless transmission exceed the energy and bandwidth budgets of smartglasses. We present EventHOI, an event-driven sensing and compression system that couples selective RGB capture with HOI-aware encoding to enable egocentric logging over Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) while preserving downstream HOI logging performance. Our key insight is to use low-power event sensing both to determine when RGB capture is needed and to identify where visual detail must be preserved. A lightweight IMU-based egomotion cancellation pipeline suppresses egomotion-induced events so that residual HOI motion can guide RGB triggering and spatial compression. We build a smartglasses prototype and conduct an end-to-end evaluation of EventHOI on a 50-hour egocentric benchmark with 97 subjects and a 20-hour real-world dataset we collect from 10 participants, together covering a broad range of daily-life scenarios and environments. Compared to RGB-only baselines, EventHOI reduces always-on backend power consumption by 5.8-10.4x and uplink bandwidth by 2.9x, with minimal HOI recognition accuracy loss. The resulting RGB uplink of less than 130 kbps fits within commodity BLE bandwidth budgets, making stable BLE video streaming feasible for egocentric HOI logging. Demo video and project website: https://eventhoi.github.io
item.dc:creator: Le Zhang, Kailai Cui, Hao Chen, Vlad Roznyatovskiy, Jianzhong Zhang, Anhong Guo, Kang G. Shin, Ke Sun

item.title: RAG-Enhanced LLMs for Interactive Explainability in Clinical Decision Support Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.09232v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in high-risks decision-making systems across domains such as healthcare, finance, and the judicial system. As reliance on predictive models grows, so does the demand for Explainable AI (XAI) to ensure transparency, trust, and interpretability. However, existing XAI approaches often fail to present explanations in a format accessible to domain experts, limiting their practical utility. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a bridge between complex models and end-users, offering natural language explanations. Yet, their use introduces new risks, including hallucinated outputs and lack of source traceability. To address these challenges, we propose a Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) that not only combines standard predictive models with XAI techniques but also incorporates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation module as an interactive enhancer. This module grounds explanations in verified medical knowledge, reformulates technical outputs into a human-like format, and enables users-such as clinicians-to actively query the system. By fostering an interactive, human-in-the-loop environment, our approach empowers domain experts to explore model decisions, contextualize explanations, and build trust in AI-assisted diagnostics. The study concludes with preliminary experiments validating the proposed methodology.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Communications in Computer and Information Science, vol. 2830, pp. 50-63 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Lorenzo Mannocci, Francesca Naretto, Lucia Passaro, Anna Monreale

item.title: Navigating Complexity: A User-Centered Evaluation of Project Management Tools
item.description: arXiv:2611.09260v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In the age of digital transformation, companies are increasingly relying on specialized software to manage the complexity of projects. However, when selecting tools, features and costs often take precedence over user experience (UX), leading to low adoption rates, user frustration, and project delays. This study empirically evaluates the user experience of leading project management tools (Jira, Trello, Monday.com, Asana, and Microsoft Project) across various project scales using a mixed methods approach. The System Usability Scale (SUS) was used as the primary quantitative instrument, with data collected from 141 experienced professionals via online questionnaires. The results reveal a significant trade-off between functionality and usability. Trello achieved the highest SUS score (77.5), indicating a superior user experience for small projects and agile teams, while Microsoft Project scored the lowest (51.2), suggesting significant usability challenges despite its robust features. Jira demonstrated a balanced profile, offering powerful features with manageable complexity. Statistical analyses confirmed that the choice of the optimal tool is highly context dependent, with team size and project complexity influencing UX outcomes. The findings underscore that UX is not a secondary feature but a critical success factor for software acceptance and project effectiveness. This study provides an evidence-based framework for aligning tool selection with the project context, offers practitioners actionable insights, and identifies design opportunities for software developers.
item.dc:creator: Yasin Ghadimi Zaker, Hamid Reza Ghaeini

item.title: Tracybot: Preserving Developer Intent by Tracing Agent-Generated Code to Prompts
item.description: arXiv:2611.09395v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used in software development, and LLM-based coding agents are given increasing autonomy. With coding agents, many design decisions are made in the conversation between the developer and the agent. Typically, the developer starts a conversation with an agent and states their intent, the agent proposes options if needed, and the developer plans the change accordingly. Then, the resulting code is committed. However, in such scenarios, the decisions and the intent behind the changes remain in the conversation, with no link to the code they produced. In this paper, we present Tracybot, an open-source tool that integrates with VS Code, Git, and coding agents to keep track of relevant conversations in an LLM-assisted development process. Tracybot captures each change as a Tasklet which consists of optional planning prompts used to plan a change, together with a build prompt that produces it. Tracybot has two main features: (i) it maps line-level code changes made by coding agents to the Tasklets that produced them, and (ii) it allows the developer to export a Tasklet as a decision record when needed, for example when the decision concerns the architecture of the project. We developed the tool over two iterations of a design science study, while focusing the evaluation on the usability and user-friendliness of the tool. In a focus group (7 participants) and a survey (24 participants), we found that Tracybot was perceived as useful for activities like code review, and most participants found our Tasklet design and presentation to be a clear way to represent the developer's intent. Tool: https://github.com/TracyTeam/tracybot. Video: https://youtu.be/Vg_a1F5eO04.
item.dc:creator: R\u{a}zvan Albu, Aliaksei Khval, Maxine Orlova, Danis Music, Filipe Ara\'ujo Veras Rosa, Lirong Yi, Ranim Khojah

item.title: Uniqueness-Aware Feature Engineering for Representing Humans in Algorithmic Decision Making
item.description: arXiv:2611.09403v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fairness analyses of algorithmic decision systems typically treat the feature representation of individuals as an a priori fixed input. How well a feature representation captures what is actually decision-relevant for different people and their unique backgrounds, however, is typically left unexamined. We address this gap by modeling feature engineering as a stochastic selection process over the pooled characteristics as candidate features for a finite training population. Based on this model, we develop a new framework for uniqueness-aware feature engineering which operates in two layers. The first layer measures population heterogeneity using a multivariate hypergeometric model of feature prevalence. It shows how well an individual is represented by any given input representation and which individual of the population is "least represented" compared to their personal, reference characteristics. The second layer acts on this assessment using set-similarity measures to search for an optimum between representational fit of the population and predictive accuracy. Without assuming prior knowledge about unseen individuals, our framework grants represented humans agency over what counts as decision-relevant in their case, gives deploying institutions accountability through a publishable representation fit report, and provides each person subject to a decision transparency about their personal representation fit. We operationalize our framework as a six-step pipeline and show a proof-of-principle using synthetic data. Our approach offers a blueprint for making algorithmic decision systems accountable for how well they represent individuals during development and in production.
item.dc:creator: Theresa Elstner, Martin Potthast

item.title: What to Delegate, What to Preserve: Human Preferences for Agentic AI Across Everyday Life and Work
item.description: arXiv:2611.09730v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI agents can execute multi-step tasks on users' behalf, yet the boundaries of acceptable delegation remain unclear. We report a scenario-based survey of 289 U.S. adults with prior AI experience covering 45 use cases across nine life domains. Each respondent evaluated one scenario per domain, producing repeated measures of automation preference, trust, collaboration, AI leadership, privacy concern, and willingness to pay. Automation preferences varied substantially across domains. Generalized estimating equation models showed that greater trust in the AI agent, desired AI leadership, prior task-specific AI use, and anticipated financial savings were associated with greater automation preference. In contrast, concerns that automation would reduce personal fulfillment predicted lower automation preference. Open-ended responses further revealed a preference for bounded autonomy, with participants often favoring substantial AI execution while retaining human involvement, oversight, or final authority. We argue that delegation is best understood as a configuration of execution, collaboration, leadership, and authority.
item.dc:creator: Sarah Wheeler, Veronica Rammouz, Yaoyao Qian, Zexuan Liu, Mengyi Wei, Anthony Rios, Tianzhi He, Kyrie Zhou

item.title: Assessing the Impact of Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Algorithmic Problem-Solving
item.description: arXiv:2611.09791v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Competitive programming problems pose distinctive challenges for Large Language Models, as they demand not only proficient code generation but also advanced algorithmic reasoning. This study presents a Retrieval-Augmented Generation approach specifically designed to enhance the capacity of Large Language Models to address such problems. Our approach integrates an embedding-based retrieval mechanism and a similarity search algorithm to identify analogous problems within a knowledge database, employing a dynamically adjusted threshold to mitigate retrieval noise. We conducted an evaluation using the CodeContests dataset, focusing on the test split problems that exhibit similarity to instances from the training split. The experimental framework considered three conditions: (i) problems provided solely with their original descriptions, (ii) problems supplemented with randomly selected examples from the training split, and (iii) problems augmented with similar examples retrieved through the proposed method. In addition, we incorporated a Min-K membership inference analysis to examine whether the generated code solutions were influenced by potential memorization of training data within the evaluated Large Language Models. This complementary perspective enables a deeper understanding of model behavior by distinguishing genuine generalization through retrieval from implicit recall of pretraining samples. Performance was assessed using both pass rates and the CodeForces Elo rating of the problems. The results provide empirical evidence that similarity-based retrieval substantially enhances Large Language Models performance in competitive programming scenarios, offering an scalable framework for improving code generation in algorithmic problem-solving contexts.
item.dc:creator: Gabriel Souza Baggio, Gabriel Machado Lunardi, Guilherme Medeiros Machado, Subhankar Maity, Faiza Belbachir, Jos\'e Palazzo Moreira de Oliveira

item.title: HexTiles and Semantic Icons for MAUP-Aware Multivariate Geospatial Visualizations
item.description: arXiv:2407.16897v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce HexTiles, a hexagonal-tiling based visual encoding design for multivariate geospatial data. Visualizing several geospatial variables at once is difficult because map position is already reserved for geography, and because variables are often reported on different, irregular spatial units whose aggregation is subject to the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP). HexTiles bins data of differing spatial discretizations into hierarchical hexagons and encodes up to three variables per tile in a base color, an inner ring, and semantic icons whose count conveys value, letting the visualization designer guide attention to specific variables and their interactions. To make the effects of MAUP visible, we compute a spatially-weighted variance for each variable within each tile and encode it as a confidence value in every channel, so that the variability hidden by aggregation is not lost. Because interactive maps are increasingly viewed in tilted, 3D perspective, HexTiles encodes quantitative values only in channels that perspective does not distort, namely color and icon count. In a user study comparing HexTiles to Square-glyphs, participants rated HexTiles as significantly less demanding and frustrating, and performed more consistently with it. Domain experts in ecology and hydrology further noted its value for communicating regional patterns, and that the confidence encoding signals where aggregated values should be interpreted with care. Our results suggest that, although 3D is commonly discouraged, it can work for multivariate geospatial visualization when restricted to perspective-robust channels.
item.dc:creator: Yuya Kawakami, Sarah Yuniar, Kwan-Liu Ma

item.title: Situating the Development of Conversational Artificial Intelligence in the Social and Structural Contexts of People with Visual Impairments
item.description: arXiv:2510.12268v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: People with visual impairments (PVI) increasingly adopt conversational AI (CAI) in their daily practices. While much existing HCI research has focused on the technical capabilities of CAI, less has examined the societal contexts in which PVI use CAI, particularly from non-Western perspectives. We conducted a study with 14 participants with visual impairments in South Korea using an audio-based probe featuring imagined dialogues between a blind user and a future CAI. Our findings situate CAI use alongside persistent social barriers such as prejudice and restricted employment opportunities that contribute to a lack of social visibility for PVI. These societal conditions shape not only how CAI is used, but also how the potential benefits and limitations of CAI are experienced. We discuss the need for CAI design within the socio-technical realities of PVI, and conclude by discussing the importance of emphasizing social awareness and empowerment in the development of future CAI systems.
item.dc:creator: Jeanne Choi, Dasom Choi, Sejun Jeong, Hwajung Hong, Joseph Seering

item.title: AURA: A Reinforcement Learning Framework for AI-Driven Adaptive Conversational Surveys
item.description: arXiv:2510.27126v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conventional online surveys provide limited personalization, often resulting in low engagement and superficial responses. Although AI survey chatbots improve convenience, most are still reactive: they rely on fixed dialogue trees or static prompt templates and therefore cannot adapt within a session to fit individual users, which leads to generic follow-ups and weak response quality. We address these limitations with AURA (Adaptive Understanding through Reinforcement Learning for Assessment), a reinforcement learning framework for AI-driven adaptive conversational surveys. AURA quantifies response quality using a four-dimensional LSDE metric (Length, Self-disclosure, Emotion, and Specificity) and selects follow-up question types via an epsilon-greedy policy that updates the expected quality gain within each session. Initialized with priors extracted from 96 prior campus-climate conversations (467 total chatbot-user exchanges), the system balances exploration and exploitation across 10-15 dialogue exchanges, dynamically adapting to individual participants in real time. In controlled evaluations, AURA achieved a +0.076 mean gain in response quality and a statistically significant improvement over non-adaptive baselines (p=0.044, d=0.66), driven by a 63% reduction in specification prompts and a 10x increase in validation behavior. These results demonstrate that reinforcement learning can give survey chatbots improved adaptivity, transforming static questionnaires into interactive, self-improving assessment systems.
item.dc:creator: Jinwen Tang, Yi Shang

item.title: Human-AI Collaboration in Large Language Model-Integrated Building Energy Management Systems: The Role of User Domain Knowledge and AI Literacy
item.description: arXiv:2602.16140v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This study aimed to comprehend how user domain knowledge and artificial intelligence (AI) literacy impact the effective use of human-AI interactive building energy management system (BEMS). While prior studies have investigated the potential of integrating large language models (LLMs) into BEMS or building energy modeling, very few studies have examined how user interact with such systems. We conducted a systematic role-playing experiment, where 85 human subjects interacted with an advanced generative pre-trained transformer (OpenAI GPT-4o). Participants were tasked with identifying the top five behavioral changes that could reduce home energy use with the GPT model that functioned as an LLM-integrated BEMS. Then, the collected prompt-response data and participant conclusions were analyzed using an analytical framework that hierarchically assessed and scored human-AI interactions and their home energy analysis approaches. Also, participants were classified into four groups based on their self-evaluated domain knowledge of building energy use and AI literacy, and Kruskal-Wallis H tests with post-hoc pairwise comparisons were conducted across 20 quantifiable metrics. Key takeaways include: most participants employed concise prompts (median: 16.2 words) and relied heavily on GPT's analytical capabilities; and notably, only 1 of 20 metrics, appliance identification rate, showed statistically significant group differences (p=0.037), driven by AI literacy rather than domain knowledge, suggesting an equalizing effect of LLMs across expertise levels. This study provides foundational insights into human-AI collaboration dynamics and promising development directions in the context of LLM-integrated BEMS and contributes to realizing human-centric LLM-integrated energy systems.
item.dc:creator: Wooyoung Jung, Kahyun Jeon, Prosper Babon-Ayeng

item.title: A\"ira: Rethinking AI Research Assistants for Interdisciplinary Science
item.description: arXiv:2607.12736v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific discovery increasingly depends on interdisciplinary teams whose members contribute distinct expertise, conceptual frameworks, vocabularies, assumptions, and standards of evidence. Today's AI research assistants are largely designed to support individual researchers through literature review, writing assistance, coding, and data analysis. While these capabilities improve personal productivity, they provide little support for the collaborative reasoning required to integrate knowledge across disciplines. In this vision paper, we argue that AI research assistants should evolve from tools that optimize individual workflows to systems designed for interdisciplinary teams. We introduce a\"ira, an AI research assistant built around this idea. Rather than focusing solely on summarization or question answering, a\"ira identifies disciplinary perspectives, translates terminology, highlights assumptions, and synthesizes collaborative research opportunities. This paper offers a vision describing the design principles underlying a\"ira, presenting its system architecture, illustrating its outputs through interdisciplinary research meetings, and outlining future research directions for AI systems that support collaborative scholarship.
item.dc:creator: Diya Mirji, Tiffany Degbotse, Sharmil Nanjappa, Jiayi Zhou, Vishnu Manoj, Vihaan Nama, Boyuan Chen, Lee Tiedrich, Christopher Bail, David W. Johnston, Walter Sinnott-Armstrong, Brinnae Bent

item.title: The As-If Machine: Personalized AI counterfactuals make distant policy risks feel close
item.description: arXiv:2610.33301v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Life experiences can shape policy attitudes, but we only live one life. Citizens may therefore fail to support policies addressing risks they have never personally experienced. Narratives can make such risks immediate and personal, but personalized stories remain difficult to produce at scale. Here we ask whether AI can make distant scenarios feel concrete by simulating a participant's life as if that scenario occurred. We present the As-If Machine (AIM), a multi-agent system through which people co-write personalized counterfactual narratives---stories about their own lives under different policy futures. In two pre-registered and quota-matched experiments on science funding (N=1,007) and satellite cybersecurity (N=894), we compared AIM with two controls: reading an expert-written vignette on the same topic and co-writing with AIM about an unrelated topic. AIM increased psychological closeness---how close a risk feels to the self---by nearly identical margins in the two domains (0.36 and 0.38 standard deviations (SDs) against the vignette, 0.80 and 0.90 against unrelated writing). AIM increased psychological closeness even among participants with unfavorable views of AI. For policy attitudes, AIM's effects were 0.16 SDs against the vignette and 0.10 SDs (n.s.) against unrelated writing for science funding; the corresponding effects for satellite cybersecurity were 0.54 and 0.67 SDs. Across 23,496 human-AI autocomplete interactions, participants and the system played distinct roles: AIM supplied concrete detail that grounded the scenario, and participants supplied first-person perspective and emotion. Co-writing with the As-If Machine makes distant policy risks feel close.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Ashkinaze, Yubo Zhou, Pengyu Chen, Avi Bhattacharya, Hyebin Park, Yanman Zhang, Stephanie Preston, Eric Gilbert, Ceren Budak

item.title: Making Sense of Audience Change: Causal Attribution and Boundary Management on Xiaohongshu
item.description: arXiv:2610.38026v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recommendation-driven platforms can reshape not only what users see, but also who becomes visible and how community boundaries are negotiated. We examine Xiaohongshu discussions surrounding a perceived World Cup-related audience influx to understand how users attributed community change and how those explanations related to boundary-management strategies. We analyzed 262 comments from eight high-engagement threads using researcher-led thematic analysis, structured coding, and permutation-based association analysis. Users described personalization as both social separation and a boundary that could fail, interpreted platform growth through audience acquisition and commercialization, and contested whether gender should define community membership. Among 70 comments with explicit attributions and strategies, attribution and strategy were strongly associated (Cramer's V = .583): algorithmic attributions concentrated in technical boundary management, while social-actor attributions more often aligned with social enforcement or normative socialization. These findings connect causal sensemaking with boundary management and show how audience restructuring can create governance consequences on recommendation-driven platforms.
item.dc:creator: Erin Zhou, Kyrie Zhou

item.title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
item.description: arXiv:2611.06346v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: At work, people develop skills through experience: novices acquire skills by completing tasks, while experts retain theirs through continued practice. AI assistance changes this process by offering workers a choice between solving tasks independently and accepting the AI's answers. While relying on AI saves immediate effort, it can also displace the practice needed to acquire and retain skills, including those required to oversee the AI. We extend an existing accept-or-solve model to a sequence of tasks in which workers' skills evolve through independent practice and reliance on AI. We compare myopic workers, who maximize immediate utility, with strategic workers, who also value their future skills. We show that novices can become trapped at low skill levels, while experts may lose skill, even as AI-assisted outcome accuracy remains high. Strategic workers, by contrast, may choose to solve independently even when AI is more accurate, recognizing the future value of acquiring and retaining their skills. We then study incentives that reward correct independent work and characterize the payments needed to encourage skill acquisition and retention. We show that independent work can become self-sustaining once workers acquire sufficient skill, eliminating the need for continued incentives. Counterintuitively, supporting a higher skill target can sometimes reduce long-run incentive costs, either by enabling self-sustaining independent work or by lowering the payments needed to maintain proficiency. Our findings thereby shift the focus from whether workers should rely on AI on individual tasks to how organizations can sustain human expertise over time, and which skills are worth investing in.
item.dc:creator: Moritz Diener, Daniel Hendriks, Philipp Spitzer, Gerhard Satzger, Joshua Holstein, Wei Sun

item.title: Same Words, Different Judgments: How Preferences Vary Across Modalities
item.description: arXiv:2602.22710v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) is the dominant framework for aligning AI systems to human preferences. However, evaluation protocols for such data were designed for text and have not been validated for speech. We present the first intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC)-based, controlled cross-modal study of human and synthetic preference annotations, comparing text and audio evaluations of identical semantic content across 100 prompts. We show that achieving \textit{good} (audio) to \textit{near good} (text) agreement within either modality (ICC(2,$k$) $\approx$ .81 audio, .74 text) requires $\sim$9 raters and modalities show marked differences in how people report preferences: audio raters exhibit narrower decision thresholds, reduced length bias, and more user-oriented evaluation criteria, with near-chance cross-modality agreement. We demonstrate that synthetic ratings can be used to effectively predict inter-rater agreement, thus serving as an early signal for stimulus selection and proxy for human annotations. Together, these findings argue that evaluation protocols for audio preference data require modality-specific design rather than direct adaptation from text. Code, data, and the audio corpus are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/sciminds/same-words-different-judgements
item.dc:creator: Aaron Broukhim, Nadir Weibel, Eshin Jolly

item.title: Intentmaking and Sensemaking: Human Interaction with AI-Guided Mathematical Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2605.05921v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Artificial intelligence offers powerful paradigms for scientific discovery, orchestrating autonomous inner search loops over long horizons. However, discovery remains bottlenecked by the friction of the outer human-AI loop: the cycle where domain experts formulate research objectives, diagnose reward hacks, and extract meaning. We present findings from a study with 11 expert mathematicians using AlphaEvolve, an evolutionary coding agent, across more than 2,300 experiments over three months. We identify and characterize intentmaking, the iterative process of discovering, defining, and refining experimental goals through system interaction, as a reciprocal counterpart to sensemaking. We observe that domain experts effectively alternate between steering the search space (intentmaking) and extracting mathematical insights (sensemaking). Our findings suggest an approach to designing AI tools for scientific discovery that moves beyond the existing question--answer model, treating them as collaborative instruments rather than opaque black-box oracles.
item.dc:creator: Alex B\"auerle, Adam Connors, Alexander Novikov, Adam Zsolt Wagner, Ng\^an V\~u, Fernanda Viegas, Martin Wattenberg, Lucas Dixon

item.title: Evidence-Linked Radiology Reporting: A Human-Supervised Reference Architecture for Structured Imaging Intelligence
item.description: arXiv:2605.25120v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Radiology reports remain the primary mechanism by which imaging findings are communicated to clinical teams. However, much of the structured information behind these reports, including measurements, image evidence, prior comparisons, lesion identity, uncertainty, and terminology, often remains trapped in free text or fragmented across picture archiving and communication systems, radiology information systems, reporting workstations, worksheets, advanced visualization tools, and electronic health records. This paper proposes a human-supervised, evidence-linked reference architecture for structured radiology reporting. The framework combines exam-specific templates, speech-to-structure processing, measurement and segmentation capture, controlled AI-assisted drafting, and standards-based interoperability using DICOM, DICOM Structured Reporting, DICOM Segmentation, HL7 FHIR, RadLex, SNOMED CT, LOINC, and UCUM. The system is positioned not as an autonomous report generator, but as a structured intelligence layer for enterprise imaging that supports reviewed reporting, longitudinal comparison, clinical data reuse, governance, and integration with PACS, RIS, EHR, analytics, and registry workflows. The paper also discusses modality-specific deployment considerations, clinical safety risks, validation requirements, cybersecurity, privacy, quality management, and regulatory boundaries for AI-assisted radiology reporting systems.
item.dc:creator: Houman Kazemzadeh, Kamyar Naderi

item.title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
item.description: arXiv:2610.32955v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Personal email agents decide, for every message, its type and urgency and whether to draft a reply, create a task or ignore it. In production these decisions are delegated to a generative LLM or to rules, and their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We describe Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent, and a measurement protocol -- stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, secret redaction, human labels in the review loop -- that produces ground truth before any training. On 231 emails in Italian and English we compare eleven systems: the production rules, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local and hosted typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble, Jeva, Jev) and generative LLMs (Qwen2.5, Gemma 4). Four results. The production rules for message type score 28% against a 57% majority class. With about two hundred labels a logistic regression has the highest accuracy on every field (type 0.79, urgency 0.74, needs-reply 0.83, is-noise 0.90) at a latency three orders of magnitude lower, though it never predicts the two rarest types; the best zero-shot system reaches 0.74 on type. The sender's relationship to the owner is recovered from other emails of the same contact with 98.6% accuracy on the 63% of emails whose sender was seen before: it belongs in the contact graph, not in the prompt. Per-email accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the baseline ignores 18% of the emails that needed a reply or a task, against 4% for the best generative model; a cost-chosen threshold cuts that to 6% and makes the classifier the cheapest system at every price. An adversarial third round (722 emails) with eleven pre-registered hypotheses confirms seven and refutes four. Two blind annotators agree with the reference at kappa 0.81 and 0.86 on type. We release the protocol and the harness; the emails stay private.
item.dc:creator: Federico Lucca
